# Data {#sec-data}

```{r}
#| include: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# load libraries
library(xml2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggpubr)
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)
library(ggplot2)


# load dataset
df <- read.delim('../data/JPR robbery.tab', header = T, sep="\t")
ddi <- read_xml("../data/JPR robbery-ddi.xml")   # use your file's name
xml_ns_strip(ddi)                  # removes the namespace so the paths below work

vars <- xml_find_all(ddi, ".//var")

data_dict <- data.frame(
  name  = xml_attr(vars, "name"),
  label = xml_text(xml_find_first(vars, "./labl")),
  type  = xml_attr(xml_find_first(vars, "./varFormat"), "type")
)

# clean dataset
df_cleaned <- df %>% drop_na()

df_cleaned <- df_cleaned %>% select(!c(llnrobberyrate, lngdpsq, country, name, period, year, flldummyrobbery, incratioalltoptobot))

y <- df_cleaned$lnrobberyrate
X <- as.matrix(df_cleaned %>% select(!c(lnrobberyrate)))
```

The dataset comes from Inequality and Violent Crime: Evidence from Data on Robbery and Violent Theft by Eric Neumayer [@data-paper] with the replication data found on Harvard Dataverse [@data]. Each row represents a country during a specific year, and there are `r nrow(df)` rows. The variables of interest include:

1.  the Gini coefficient,
2.  the log of the gross domestic product (GDP) per capita,
3.  the growth rate of the GDP,
4.  the unemployment rate,
5.  the urbanization rate,
6.  the female labor force participation rate,
7.  the proportion of males between the ages of 15 and 64,
8.  the Polity measure of democracy,
9. the human rights violation scale, and
10. the natural log of the number of robberies and violent thefts per million people which is the response in this study.

The dataset is compiled from a variety of sources. The Gini coefficients come from the UN-WIDER database, and 6.6 is added to the values from expenditure rather than income [@data-paper]. The ratio fo the top to bottom quintile of the income distribution (data taken from A New Data Set Measuring Income Inequality by Deininger & Squire [@income-ineq]) is used to measure income inequality[@data-paper]. The rest of the data are from the UN and the World Bank [@data-paper].

There are `r sum(is.na(df))` NA values in the dataset. After dropping those values, the dataset include `r nrow(df_cleaned)` rows, which is a large difference. Table 1 shows the number of NA values in each column of interest.

| Variable | Number of NA values |
|:-----------------------------------------------|----------------------:|
|  Gini coefficient | `r sum(is.na(df['giniwider']))` |
| Log of the GDP per capita | `r sum(is.na(df['lngdp']))` |
| GDP growth rate | `r sum(is.na(df['econgrowth']))` |
| unemployment rate | `r sum(is.na(df['emtotunemimputed']))` |
| urbanization rate | `r sum(is.na(df['urban']))` |
| female labor force participation rate | `r sum(is.na(df['femlabourpart']))` |
| proportion of males between the ages of 15 and 64 | `r sum(is.na(df['male1564']))` |
| Measure of democracy | `r sum(is.na(df['politypositiveonly']))` |
| Human rights violation scale | `r sum(is.na(df['humanrightsviol']))` |
| Natural log of the number of robberies and violent thefts per million people | `r sum(is.na(df['lnrobberyrate']))` |

: This table shows the number of NA values in the columns of each variable of interest.

```{r fig-rel, fig.width=8, fig.height=7}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-cap: "Plot (a) shows a scatter plot showing the positive relationship between the GDP (x-axis) and robbery rate (y-axis). Plot (b) shows a scatter plot showing the negative relationship between the human rights violation scale (x-axis) and robbery rate (y-axis). Plot (c) shows a scatter plot showing the near constant relationship between female labor participation (x-axis) and robbery rate (y-axis)."

pos <- ggplot(data=df_cleaned, aes(x=lngdp, y=lnrobberyrate)) + 
  geom_point(color='plum4') +
  labs(x="GDP", y="Robbery Rate", title="Comparison of robbery rate versus GDP (a)") + 
  theme_minimal()

neg <- ggplot(data=df_cleaned, aes(x=humanrightsviol, y=lnrobberyrate)) +
  geom_point(color='plum4') +
  labs(x="Human Rights Violations", y="Robbery Rate", title="Comparison of robbery rate versus human\nrights violations (b)") + 
  theme_minimal()

const <- ggplot(data=df_cleaned, aes(x=femlabourpart, y=lnrobberyrate)) + 
  geom_point(color='plum4') +
  labs(x="Female labor participation", y="Robbery Rate", title="Comparison of robbery rate versus female labor participation (c)") + 
  theme_minimal()

(pos + neg) / const
```

Many of the variables show a positive linear relationship with robbery rate, with some more intuitive than others. Among such variables are GDP, democracy score, proportion of males aged 15-64, percent living in urban areas, and unemployment rate. @fig-rel (a) shows a scatter plot of the relationship between GDP and robbery rate. While it may seem unintuitive that richer countires would have a higher robbery rate, it could be due to the rising value of items being stolen and higher reporting of crimes [@data-paper]. The variables human rights scale and gdp growth show a negative relationship against robbery rates. This is shown in @fig-rel (b) for human rights violation scale. A constant relationship is seen for Gini coefficient and female labor participation with the latter depicted in @fig-rel (c). Both of these contrast with the original paper and may be due to dropped the NA values.
